$comment: Only the keys below are merged into ~/.claude/settings.json. Everything else in that file
is left untouched, including env.OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS which holds a plaintext API key.
Hook entries are appended alongside existing ones (rtk, notify-stop), never replacing them.
$comment-opinionKeys: Two kinds of key live in this file, and they do not deserve the same consent.
`hooks` is the mechanism: without it nothing in this toolkit runs, so installing it is the whole
point of running the installer. Everything named in $opinionKeys is an opinion about how OTHER
skills behave on this machine -- which telemetry is verbose, which of the bundled and plugin
Both are merged by `setup.sh install`. `install --no-opinions` merges the mechanism only.
The default was the other way round for a while, on the theory that installing a verification
gate is not consent to changing how other skills behave. That is right for a stranger, and this
toolkit has one user, who wrote these opinions. What opt-in actually bought was retyping a flag
on every machine. The distinction is still worth keeping in the file -- `--no-opinions` is the
spelling for a machine where the bundled skills should be left alone.
scripts/setup.sh reads the list from here rather than keeping its own copy: a second copy is a
second thing to forget when a key is added.
$comment-skillOverrides: Claude Code ships a large set of skills compiled into its own binary, and an Anthropic-managed
plugin adds more. None of those exist on disk, so far more names are reachable than the count in
~/.agents/skills. No figures here on purpose: this comment said 24/75, the README said 21/72, and
the real number was 23. /doctor and /skill-doctor see the actual set.
These entries either collide with something here on nearly identical triggers, or spend listing
budget on work outside the development loop.
'name-only' keeps the skill listed and still invocable but drops the description -- the part that
competes for auto-invocation. 'off' hides it from both the model and the menu.
Nothing here targets our own skills. Those live in Cursor too, and this file does not, so hiding
one here would make the two agents disagree; ours are managed by frontmatter instead. Bundled and
plugin skills do not exist in Cursor at all, so there is nothing to diverge from.
disableBundledSkills is deliberately NOT used: it drops all ~40 at once, including code-review and
review which the usage log shows in real use, and it exists only in CLI 2.1.219+ -- an older
`claude` on $PATH ignores it silently. See docs/decisions.md.
$comment-timeouts: The timeouts are declared, not left to the harness default, because a hook killed by the
harness exits with neither 0 nor 2 -- and that is non-blocking. A slow suite would turn the
gate into a silent pass, which is the one failure mode the gate exists to prevent.
900 because this repository's own profile now budgets 600s (it gates every suite check.sh runs)
and a single check may overshoot by its own timeout, the largest being 180s. 600 + 180 = 780, so
900 is strictly larger with room. Our clock has to be the one that fires -- a timeout we cause is
an event we can observe, record and block on; one the harness causes exits non-blocking and says
It is stated rather than left implicit because the documented default (600s for a command hook) is
a default, not a guarantee. An earlier version set 420, which was both below that default and
exactly equal to the gate's worst case at the time, so the two could fire together. Raising
timeout_total in any profile means raising this to match -- scripts/test-setup.sh asserts the gap.
The lint hook only reads frontmatter through node, so 15s is already far more than it needs.
